P1.evidence: KFS-set call and no setter notes read back — nothing about the application, and the prospect is addressed as 'Tom' in the opening line and 'Anthony' later, which is the opposite of feeling seen. The frame ran three parts: 'Where are you today? You know, where do you want to be? If we can help, there's so many different options that we have.' Agreement was sought for the call rather than the frame ('Shall we just jump into it?' — 'Sure'). Open question ran cleanly: 'How can we essentially help you?'

P2.evidence: Work was the one thorough piece — barber to prison barber manager, the 7:30-3:30 shift, the 4:30 alarm, the hour it creates — and the rep correctly connected the occupation to the shoulder. Age was asked, but incidentally and eighteen minutes in, mid-way through pillar two ('how old are you, Antonio? 35'), with no height or weight ever. Everything else was skipped: no health-conditions question, no injury question at all despite six months of shoulder pain being volunteered in the first minute, no current training week, no results, no diet question (the nutrition detail arrived only because the prospect asked a question during the pitch), no sleep despite him volunteering a disrupted schedule, no energy question despite 'completely drained' being central to his why.

P3.evidence: The best goals work in the batch. The six-month future-pace opened it — 'Looking back at this in six months, what would make you say, man, this is one of the best decisions I've ever made?' — then the ripple question, then three separate impact-on-others probes, each of which landed somewhere new: the kids ('dad's too tired... I don't want to miss these years'), the fiancée ('she feeds off of my energy quite a bit'), and the prison ('they don't necessarily do what you tell them to do. They do what you show them'). Legacy and identity were reached without forcing. Weaker on the mechanical checks — the aesthetics-and-function one-thing question and the strength-mobility-energy fork were never put, and the reflect-back was the generic want-or-need.

P4.evidence: P4f ran early and well: 'we live in the digital age, right? TikTok, AI, chat GBT, YouTube, Google. Why not come up with the structure yourself as opposed to using a coach like Trevor?' Then 'Why do you feel like accountability is useful for you?' produced the whole root cause in the prospect's own words — 'I'm able to just kind of get in that willpower... and then, you know, life happens, but I don't have the system set in place. And then my accountability takes a hit and then I fail.' The rep named it back cleanly ('the fuel you're using to be consistent is willpower. And willpower isn't a consistent fuel'). What did not run was the concrete history — what he actually tried, when, and what happened each time.

P5.evidence: The only consequence-adjacent work anywhere in this batch, and it ran backwards in time rather than forwards: 'if you had that in your back pocket, like everything you mentioned, say, I don't know, five years ago when you were 30, what would you say you'd be today?' — which produced 'I wouldn't need you if I had this five years ago'. That is a regret frame, not a cost-of-inaction frame. The forward two-year question never came, nor 'is that something you're willing to settle for', nor 'why not', nor the line in the sand. The prospect supplied the missing pressure himself — 'it hurts more to be where I'm at than it does to make a change' — and it was never converted.

P6.evidence: The belief question ran properly and before price: 'the most important question is, do you believe you can make this work? Are you capable of being a great student?' answered with 'I definitely think I do. I think I'm at that point now where there's really no other option.' The trust scale was also attempted, though the prospect never actually returned a number and the rep let that go. The decisive omission is P6b — the all-in question, 'if you had everything you needed, is there any reason you wouldn't go all in on this?', was never asked. Had it run, the money blocker would have surfaced before the offer rather than after it, and the whole discount ladder that followed would have been unnecessary.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted across four different price points and none of it converted, so no payment, no Trevor booking, no agreement email or signature and no welcome-email, Skool-link or questionnaire instruction. The onboarding sequence was described in advance as part of the pitch ('I give you immediate access to the platform... And what I'll also do for you is book you into a one-on-one call with Trevor') but never executed.

objection_plays.detail: Started better than any other call in the batch and then abandoned the play for a discount. The isolation ran, pre-emptively and well — 'just before we wrap up, just so I'm on the same page, when you guys have a discussion, what's the main obstacle that could maybe prevent you from doing this?' — which produced 'it will be the price'. A high-level probe followed: 'would the 650 really put you guys in a tough spot?'. Then it stopped. No permission question, no cash on hand, no monthly surplus, no credit cards, no available credit, no used-versus-available, no investments. In place of the financial picture the rep moved the price: $4,000 for three months, then a $1,200 one-month trial, then $200/month. The playbook's money play contains no authority to move price, and the moves that would have made moving price unnecessary were the ones skipped.

The strongest OB attempt in the batch. The rep checked whether she knew about the call, discovered she was in the room, and offered to bring her in with a precedent story — 'I spoke to someone literally yesterday, it was the same situation... his wife just asked all the questions that were on her mind. So she was like part of the process'. He also pre-framed the obstacle before the couple's conversation. Missing: 'money aside, do you personally feel this CAN get you to your goal', 'is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger and less in pain', the is-this-input-or-permission question, the responsibility question, and the deposit-with-full-refund fallback. The $1,200 'love it or leave it' functions as an improvised substitute for that last move, at a price that is not on the rate card.

Clear trigger — 'I really got to wait for the paychecks to get where they're supposed to be at', plus milestones 'months and months down the line'. None of the moves ran: nothing about things never slowing down, nothing about when it actually becomes the right time, nothing about the cost of waiting compounding. The rep agreed with the premise: 'As I said, that's the plan. We have a plan for the future.'

Two gaps. First, there is no scripted path for a prospect who is fully sold and genuinely cannot pay — belief was maxed ('I have no doubt that I'm going to like it when I try it', 'I can justify the cost') and capacity was zero, which OC does not contemplate. Second, and more serious, there is no governance whatsoever on descending the price. Within four minutes the rep offered a three-month tier, a one-month paid trial and a monthly subscription, at least two of which he indicated the company no longer offers. That is a policy vacuum, not a rep failure, and it needs writing down.

notes: Discovery and root cause were genuinely excellent here — the willpower-versus-system diagnosis was the best coaching moment in the batch — and the money handling undid it. The single highest-leverage fix is P6b: asking 'if you had everything you needed, is there any reason you wouldn't go all in?' before quoting would have surfaced a hard cash constraint pre-offer, instead of producing a four-step discount ladder after it.
